This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blanks must be properly filled in every case. If the information called for on any part of the blank is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parents are living or dead, their names must be given. The person who signs the blank as pertaining to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. The laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. This form is to be used only in transfers from reservations or Indian schools to nonreservation schools. CASE RECORD. 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Indian Agency, Nespelem, Wash., Oct. 23, 1919. Supt. E. H. Hammond, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington. Dear Mr. Hammond: From funds to the credit of Lawrence Covington there were purchased four yearling heifers at $45.00 each. To cover this purchase I have drawn check #4135 in the sum of $180., payable to his order. I will thank you to obtain his endorsement and return the check to me, so that an official receipt for the amount can be made out and given to the mother. Very truly yours, Fred C Morgan Superintendent. SJ-Encl. Check for $180.00 for Lawrence Curry tour Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Oct. 30, 1919 Mr. Fred C. Morgan, Supt. Colville Indian Agency Nespelem, Wash. Dear Mr. Morgan: In compliance with your request of October 23rd, I am returning herewith the check, No. 435, properly endorsed by Lawrence Covington. Very respectfully, Superintendent. /MG Enc. Cushman Indian School, Tecoma, Wash. Nov. 8, 1918. Mr. Joe Monaghan, Keller, Washington, Dear Sir: I have your inquiry of the 4th instant regarding Lawrence Beacon (Covington) would advise that he is well and is my orderly in the office every day so that I know how he is getting along. Lawrence has at no time been seriously ill. Had he been, I would have notified you. I will do so in case he does fall ill. Lawrence is supplied with a supply of clothing, but if you desire, you may send him some spending money not to exceed four dollars a month. Sincerely yours, Superintendent Keller Wash Nov. 4, 1918, My Dear Sir, Asking you how is the advance Beaver getting along if he rich or will have not hear since he went to school if he needs any money or clothing let me know expect to hear from you soon your respectfully Joe Monaghan Pupil guessed at the figures Supt. Asst. Clerk looked up actual figures October 2, 1918. Dear uncle, I am going to write you a few lines to let you know I am well now. I was very glad to hear from you. On last of September in night we have rain many James and Mary Donald and Colt Martin and Violet Rannels they ran away before yesterday today is Tuesday they ran away to visit their many Martin over third they over there. I guess one girl got caught from that four girls 3 girls got away. I don't notice it was that girls. I will find if sometimes and how is Pete and Nancy and Ed. How is Brothers. Don't know. Over there we steal some apple we eat sometimes good food just only Nancy is here all the girls is run away all time and the two they keep moving all the time some times like the school some times I don't like it. I like to go to school sometimes I like to go home at Keller sit in one little table six in each table there lunch table almost full they house when we go to eat chow. We share of girls and boys. I guess there were away all time when gone to school. The just one thirty-eight miles to Seattle from Tacoma. There's big town I go over once. George Zunqui-tas is good fighter she got scared Zun-qui-tas all the time. I to read and But I don't to work 1 day and go to 1 day they to play foot Saturday. I guess it's down at St. Louis they going to play foot Ball School is on June 21, 1919. I was very glad when October comes I was very glad I have good to-day now playing I am third Brady I thought it was hard but is it now hard it is easy. Christmas I will be in fourth then go home. Sent it in good now then throw down who got here they give overalls they give about 7 days. They give a class I went it now just Saturday I go Town when we go to Church on Sunday All day we go in night to church. Then Boys is meant I don't like it. Some is good boys and Harry Sorumpt they do that at here at Tacoma he is good Boy now and same with Marcus Martin the good Boys now at here. Good bye. Don't close answer again. Good day to you. Good day to mother mother. From Samuel Long for CASE RECORD.
